Development

The main development standard for neon1: the principles in priority order, what each word means, how work moves from idea to release, and where the detailed rules live.

Type
Standard
Edition
1.0
Updated
November 9, 2026
For
Developers
Download PDF

This is the main development standard for neon1. It covers every project neon1 builds, for itself or for a client: websites, tools, infrastructure, automations, and AI features. It sets the principles and the order of work. The detailed rules live in the standards linked at the end, and each of them follows this one.

Principles, in priority order

When two principles pull in different directions, the higher one wins. Most of the time they agree.

#PrincipleWhat it means here
1SafetyNobody is harmed, no data is lost or exposed, and nothing irreversible happens by accident. Covers security, privacy, and data integrity
2CorrectnessIt does what it says, including in the failure cases that matter
3ValueIt solves a real need someone has today. Work that isn't needed isn't done, however interesting
4UsabilityThe intended person can do the task without help, on their device, including with assistive technology
5SimplicityThe fewest parts, dependencies, and concepts that meet the need. Easy to explain in a few sentences
6RobustnessIt degrades visibly instead of silently, recovers from failure, and can be undone
7MaintainabilitySomeone else can read it, change it, and run it without the author
8EfficiencyIt uses time, money, and computing in proportion to its value. Fast enough, cheap enough, measured before optimized
9ConsistencyIt follows the conventions of its project and of neon1, so nothing has to be relearned

A few consequences of the order:

  • A simpler design that leaves a security gap loses. A faster design that's harder to use loses unless speed is the need.
  • Efficiency matters, but it comes after people can use and maintain the thing. Optimize what's measured, not what's guessed.
  • Consistency is last because a convention should give way when it would make something unsafe, wrong, or unusable. When that happens, the convention gets updated rather than quietly broken.

Words neon1 uses, defined

These words come up often. Each one means something specific here.

WordMeaning
MatureComplete for its stated purpose, dependable in its intended workflows, documented, and recoverable. Not the same as old or large
ReadyTested in conditions like real use, with known limits written down and a way back
DoneBuilt, tested, documented, reviewed, released, and handed over. Merged alone isn't done
RobustSurvives bad input, outages, and retries without corrupting anything, and says when it fails
SimpleFew parts and few concepts. Not the same as quick to write
UsableThe intended person finishes the task without help
ValuableSomeone would notice and mind if it were gone
EfficientProportionate in time, cost, and resources to what it delivers
SecureMeets the agreed baseline for its data and risks, with evidence. Never a blanket claim

How work moves

Every piece of work follows the same order, at whatever size fits:

  1. Reproduce. Start from something that works: an existing tool, a known pattern, or the current behavior, with a baseline measured.
  2. Integrate. Connect it into the complete path a person actually uses, end to end.
  3. Enhance. Improve what real use shows is missing or weak.
  4. Unify. Once several pieces work, share their common parts and make them consistent.

Reuse comes before building. Existing tools and well-maintained open-source projects come first, checked under the technology decisions standard. Custom code covers only what nothing else does.

For a bug, the order is: reproduce it, find the cause, fix it narrowly, add a test that would have caught it, and check the behavior around it.

Maturity and version 1.0.0

Before v1.0.0, a project is under initial development, and its versions say so. v1.0.0 is reserved for the first complete, dependable release of the whole intended scope, shown to work for the people it's for. Passing tests or finishing one feature doesn't make a project 1.0.0. The versioning standard defines every version number in detail.

The detailed standards

StandardCovers
WritingEvery word neon1 writes, including code comments and commit messages
Version controlBranches, commits, merges, protection, and history
Versioning and releasesVersion numbers, tags, changelogs, and when each number goes up
Code styleNames, comments, file headers, formatting, and layout
Testing and reviewWhat gets tested, how changes are reviewed, and the definition of done
DocumentationREADMEs, changelogs, decision records, and runbooks
Security and dataThe security baseline and data handling
Design and accessibilityInterfaces and documents anyone can use
Technology decisionsChoosing tools and architecture, and counting the full cost
Reliability and recoveryService targets, backups, and incidents
AI quality and oversightAI features inside what neon1 builds

Your code is yours

Code written for a client lives in a repository the client owns, under the license agreed. The handover includes how to build, test, deploy, and roll back without me. Reused open-source code keeps its license and notices, and I explain what each license allows.

Review tools

I use AI tools to review code for bugs, security issues, and missing tests, alongside automated checks. I review and take responsibility for every change that ships. See How I use AI.
